title: Polynomial-time universality for unambiguous context-free grammars
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that decides whether \(L(G)=\Sigma^{*}\) for every context-free grammar \(G\) promised to be unambiguous, in time polynomial in the bit length of its explicit description? The algorithm must have one polynomial running-time bound on all input strings; correctness is required on the promised grammars. The terminal alphabet is part of the input. This card selects the polynomial-time endpoint of the source’s broader question about the exact complexity.
why: Unique parse trees suffice to make universality decidable, but they do not give deterministic control of parsing. A polynomial-time procedure, or a proof excluding one, would locate the computational cost of this fundamental coverage test between finite-state reasoning and general context-free behavior.
status_note: The 2019 question asks to close the complexity gap. Primary papers from 2020 and 2023 give successively stronger upper bounds, the latter in coRP with a PP oracle. A bounded search on 13 September 2026 found no resolution of the deterministic polynomial-time endpoint; this is not exhaustive current-openness certification.

progress.text: The problem list asks for improved upper or lower complexity bounds under the unambiguity promise.
Theorem 10 gives a polynomial-space algorithm; the discussion leaves exact universality complexity open.
Corollary 4 and its stated consequence place universality of arbitrary-alphabet unambiguous grammars in \(\mathrm{coRP}^{\mathrm{PP}}\), improving the polynomial-space bound.

sentences: An unambiguous context-free grammar gives each accepted word a unique parse tree.
This card asks whether a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm can test if such a grammar generates every finite word over its alphabet.
Unambiguity is promised for the supplied grammar, and the alphabet and complete production rules are part of the input.
The checked upper bound uses randomized polynomial time with a PP oracle; it does not yield the unconditional deterministic polynomial-time procedure sought here.
The polynomial-time endpoint is an explicit editorial specialization of the source’s broader complexity question, with either answer requiring a Lean-checked proof.

definitions: A context-free grammar is a finite tuple \(G=(V,\Sigma,P,S)\), where the finite sets of nonterminals \(V\) and terminals \(\Sigma\) are disjoint, \(S\in V\), and \(P\subseteq V\times(V\cup\Sigma)^{*}\) is a finite set of production rules. The alphabet is finite and nonempty. All symbols, productions and right-hand-side strings are listed explicitly with delimited binary indices; repeated identical rules are treated as a single rule. Empty right-hand sides and unit productions are allowed.

A parse tree is a finite ordered rooted tree with root \(S\). Each nonterminal node expands according to one production, with its children in the right-hand-side order; an empty production contributes no terminal. Its yield is the terminal string read from left to right. \(L(G)\) is the set of yields. The unambiguity promise says that each word has at most one such parse tree, including the empty word. It is a promise on the given grammar, not merely on its language.

Universality includes every finite word, including \(\varepsilon\). Polynomial time means that there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine and constants \(C,d\geq1\) whose runtime on every string of length \(N\) is at most \(C(N+1)^{d}\). It outputs a bit. On every well-formed unambiguous grammar this bit is 1 exactly for universal grammars; on other inputs either answer is allowed.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the specified uniform polynomial-time promise algorithm, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A faster superpolynomial algorithm, a conditional lower bound alone, or an algorithm limited to deterministic grammars does not meet this criterion.

context_blocks.text: The 2019 problem asks to close the complexity gap for universality with a unique-parse promise. The benchmark’s yes/no polynomial-time endpoint is an editorial choice; a negative answer would leave finer complexity classification open.

Clemente’s 2020 paper proves a polynomial-space upper bound (Theorem 10). Its quantitative coin-flip-measure hardness theorem concerns a different problem and does not establish an equivalent hardness result for universality.

The 2023 paper improves the checked upper bound to \(\mathrm{coRP}^{\mathrm{PP}}\): randomized polynomial time with one-sided error and access to an oracle for majority acceptance of polynomial-time nondeterministic computations. This oracle-assisted bound does not provide the deterministic polynomial-time algorithm asked for here.

statement_review.notes: Individually selected the polynomial-time endpoint of a broad complexity question and labeled it editorial.
